bearings.paper_claim: Unit fixed-effects regressions are biased when treatment and time-varying covariates feed back on each other (citing Imai & Kim 2019 and Sobel 2012). The paper's remedy moves the fixed effects into a propensity model and requires a binary treatment that switches within units, a correctly specified parametric propensity model, and N and T growing together. Simulations use n of 200-3000 with T of at least 4; in the empirical panel, campaign windows run 8-40 weeks.
bearings.system_side: Fits OLS of log giving and log lobbying on sector FE, growth, phase, tossup and trend, with variants that add year FE (variant year_fe) and a lagged/AR lobbying term, using wild cluster restricted bootstrap by sector. Brain record: the L3-LV coefficient +0.352 becomes -0.477 with sector+year FE, and the first-difference lead is -0.537 over 71 pairs.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Only the diagnosis transfers, not the estimator. The study's 'treatment' is continuous sector growth with few sector clusters and annual T, so IPTW-FE cannot run: there is no binary switching treatment and no feasible propensity model. Read the paper as support for the study's existing choice to keep the lobbying-lead results DESCRIPTIVE. A sign flip under added FE is what feedback or time-varying confounding produces, so neither sign is causal. Carries over to any sector-year panel in which lagged lobbying or giving enters as a regressor.

extraction.research_question: Have the trends identified in Congress (1997) toward polarization and one-dimensionality in roll call voting continued through the 105th Congress, and does the 1994 Republican takeover represent a sharp break? Secondary: do DW-NOMINATE and alternative scaling methods recover essentially the same legislator positions, and how does the U.S. Congress fit the spatial model compared with other legislatures? (Abstract p.2; Sec. 1 p.3.)
extraction.theory: Basic spatial theory of ideology (Ordeshook 1976; Hinich and Pollard 1981; Enelow and Hinich 1984; Hinich and Munger 1994): legislators have ideal points in a low-dimensional policy space and choose the outcome closer to them. Dynamic extension: legislator coordinates are polynomial functions of time (Appendix eq. A1, p.19). Roll call utility is a normal-error probit over a Gaussian-type distance with dimension salience weights (eqs. A2-A4, p.20).
extraction.data: U.S. House and Senate roll calls, Congresses 1-105 (1789-1998). Unit: legislator-roll call choice (Yea or Nay; abstentions discarded, endnote 9, p.30). Legislators included if they cast at least 25 votes in at least one Congress (endnote 1, p.30). House: 38,740 scalable roll calls, 10,208 scalable representatives, 10,495,639 choices (Table 1, p.23). Senate: 41,165 roll calls, 1,794 senators, 2,697,691 choices (Table 1, p.24). Joint House-Senate scaling: 79,905 roll calls, 11,389 unique legislators, 13,193,330 choices, with 613 members serving in both chambers as "glue" (Table 3, p.27; p.10). Presidents Eisenhower through Clinton included as members of both chambers using CQ presidential support roll calls (p.10). Comparison sets (Table 4, p.28-29): 105th House (946 roll calls, 443 legislators), 105th Senate (486, 101), Third and Fourth European Parliament, 1841 British Parliament, French National Assembly 1951-56, Czech Parliament 1993-97, 1995 Polish Parliament, UN General Assembly sets.
extraction.method: DW-NOMINATE (dynamic, weighted, nominal three-step estimation): normal (probit) errors replacing D-NOMINATE's logit errors; per-dimension salience weights w_k; legislator coordinates polynomial in time, estimated as constant (v=0) and linear (v=1) only (p.5-6, Appendix p.19-20). Estimated by maximum likelihood over the joint choice likelihood (eq. A4, p.20). Comparators: Poole's non-parametric optimal classification (rank ordering that maximizes correct classification; one dimension only; Poole 1997, 2000), Heckman-Snyder factor analysis (p.9). Fit measured by percent correctly classified, APRE, and geometric mean probability (Table 1 notes, p.24-25). Party polarization measured by mean within- and between-party pairwise distances (Figs 7-8, p.14) and percent party overlap (Fig 9, p.15). Joint scaling of both chambers estimated with optimal classification (Table 3, p.27).
extraction.identification: Not a causal design; this is measurement of ideal points. Ideal points are identified by maximum likelihood across roll calls with the salience weight for dimension 1 set to one and the probit error variance normalized to 1 (p.8). Linear trends are estimated for legislators serving at least 3 (or 5) Congresses; the authors concede the 3-Congress threshold lets random walkers appear linear, which biases toward the polynomial models (p.6). Joint House-Senate scaling assumes the 613 glue members hold fixed positions across chambers (p.10); the authors call this "reasonably supported" from the classification drop of about 1 point (p.11-12).
extraction.scope: Population: all roll call votes and members of the U.S. House and Senate, 1789-1998 (Congresses 1-105). Substantive focus: Post-Reconstruction Democrat/Republican party system, 1879-1998, with extra attention to recent Congresses (p.12). Cross-national comparison (Sec. 6, p.16-17): a few legislatures at single time spans. Institution: the U.S. Congress plus selected parliaments. Era: Post-Reconstruction and modern polarization (1879-1998).

Optimal classification was done only in one dimension; the two-dimensional version was deferred (p.9).

The cross-national claim that only the Czech, 1841 British and French National Assembly fit better than the 105th Congress holds on APRE and classification jointly. Figures 1-10 are not in the extracted text, so the trend claims resting on them (Figs 1B, 2B, 7-10) cannot be verified here.

The party-discipline argument depends on a 1999 working paper (McCarty, Poole and Rosenthal) that is cited but not presented (p.17). The paper contains no causal analysis, so the 1994 break is assessed only descriptively (p.14-15).

summary_md:
Poole and Rosenthal update their 1997 roll-call study through the 105th Congress (1789-1998) using DW-NOMINATE, a dynamic probit spatial model of legislator ideal points. Four results matter here. First, legislator positions are close to fixed over a career: the linear time-trend model adds only about 0.3 points of classification over the constant model (House 85.65 to 85.96; Senate 84.04 to 84.40). Second, Congress has become one-dimensional: the second dimension now adds under 1 percent. Third, party overlap on dimension 1 is near zero: under 1.5% in both chambers over the last five Congresses, and none in the last three Senates. Fourth, polarization rose smoothly, with no break at 1994. A non-parametric rank method produces nearly the same orders (Spearman .960 House, .981 Senate). The donor and primary claim that Paul highlighted in pink rests on a cited working paper that this text does not present.

For the system as built, the paper is a measurement baseline. It is not an engine input. DW-NOMINATE appears only as a control (fec/members/dw_control.py) and through per-Congress Nokken-Poole scores used as a criterion. The sharpest consequence is for the say-do gate's Path V. One CU-aligned final-passage vote counts as corroboration, and in a polarized, one-dimensional chamber that vote mostly records the member's party. A read-only check confirms strong party sorting in several categories (details in bearings). That check is UNVERIFIED. The paper also explains why drift-based susceptibility criteria have little true variance to detect. It argues for using an ideal-point control rather than a bare party dummy wherever party-confounded tiers are interpreted, as in the CFPB isolation. The paper does nothing for lobbying, money effects, pathfinding or allocation.
